items.content_text: Researchers introduce MixUA, a memory system designed to improve multi-user, multi-agent interactions by distilling independent user-agent experiences into lessons assigned to user-agent pairs, individual users, agents, or global scopes based on benefit and privacy considerations. The system aims to enhance skill sharing while preventing private information leakage across users and agents. To evaluate MixUA, the team developed CrossLearnBench, a benchmark combining agent tasks with user preferences and privacy tests. In experiments involving five users and seven agents, MixUA increased task pass rates by up to 16 points compared to no memory and 5 points over a single global memory, retained up to 90% of user preferences, and limited privacy breaches to at most 0.02% of probes. The researchers suggest MixUA could enable scalable co-evolution of users and agents in global systems.

items.title: Researchers propose QK-MAP, a magnitude-aware projection method for query-key representations in large language models that preserves token-specific magnitude information without normalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce QK-MAP, a new approach to constructing queries and keys in large language models that avoids traditional query-key normalization (QK-Norm) by encoding magnitude changes as bounded phase patterns using multiple learnable frequencies. This method maintains sensitivity to token-specific magnitude information, which QK-Norm suppresses, and controls query-key scale without discarding important attention selectivity and token importance signals. Experiments on models ranging from 190 million to 7 billion parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss compared to standard attention and QK-Norm methods. Further analysis indicates that QK-MAP preserves input scale sensitivity, reduces attention to the first token, and enhances attention contrast in synthetic long-context tests, demonstrating effective control of query-key scale while retaining meaningful magnitude information.

items.title: Researchers introduce PURL framework for Masked Diffusion Models to enable selective token revision during parallel text generation, improving accuracy by up to 47.4% and reducing decoding rounds by up to 8 times [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose Planned Unmasking-and-Revision Joint Learning (PURL), a training-based framework for Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) that integrates parallel generation with selective token revision to address inconsistent early token commitments. PURL jointly trains edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction on partially masked sequences, allowing a single forward pass during inference to decode and revise tokens. The approach shows significant accuracy improvements and efficiency gains across tasks like logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. The study reveals that effective token edits depend on the timing and context accumulation, with early edits influencing broader trajectories and later edits being more localized. These findings suggest that improving parallel generation performance relies on making the right token commitments revisable at appropriate times rather than simply increasing the number of revisions.

items.title: Researchers find language model capabilities degrade in a consistent order under compression and perturbation across multiple models and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A study applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned language models, evaluating 16 tasks to determine how individual capabilities fail under these conditions. The results showed that short-answer capabilities deteriorate in a nearly identical sequence across different random perturbations and within models under pruning and quantization, with factors like answer margin and frequency predicting this order. Fragility profiles derived from random perturbations could predict which tasks and facts are lost first due to compression and accurately forecast held-out task performance after calibration. However, this failure order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or apply to long-form tasks, indicating that while short-answer capability degradation is predictable before deployment, it varies with model type and task format.

items.title: Researchers propose phrase-level speculative decoding using a small MLP head on frozen target models to improve throughput without changing the tokenizer or target model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a phrase-level speculative decoding method that predicts one- to three-word phrases as single entries using a small MLP head on a frozen target model's hidden states, aiming to increase throughput in language generation. This approach keeps the target model and tokenizer unchanged, verifies multiple candidates in one forward pass, and produces outputs identical to greedy decoding except for floating-point tie-breaking. Evaluated on an A5000 GPU, the method achieves up to 2.44x speedup on benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH-500 compared to HuggingFace's generate() function, using a draft vocabulary significantly smaller than previous methods like EAGLE-3.

items.title: Researchers introduce HiVe-Mem, a multimodal memory framework combining horizontal memory expansion and vertical evidence composition to improve long-term interaction in multimodal agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: HiVe-Mem is a new multimodal memory system designed to enhance long-term interactions by effectively retrieving and utilizing past information. It organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors to expand semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors, while also composing query-adaptive evidence subsets from multiple forms such as summaries, captions, and raw images. The framework's two-dimensional design broadens memory coverage and adapts evidence use per query, leading to consistent task performance improvements across base models. Experiments on three multimodal memory benchmarks show HiVe-Mem reduces token consumption by about 90% compared to the most efficient competing multimodal baselines, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness in managing heterogeneous multimodal information.

items.title: Researchers release Micius-Flash, a 27-billion-parameter multimodal AI model for engineering with deep reasoning and a 256K-token context window [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Micius-Flash is a new AI model designed for engineering tasks, featuring native multimodal input, deep reasoning capabilities, and a large 256K-token context window. It integrates expert models trained on semiconductor knowledge, hardware coding, and multimodal understanding through a Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation process, achieving significant performance improvements on hardware code and semiconductor benchmarks compared to similar-sized baselines. The model is connected to industrial tools like EDA and KiCad through Micius Harness, enabling applications in PCB design, chip design automation, and software development with iterative planning and debugging capabilities. The researchers have released Micius as an open-source project to support further development of AI agents in science and engineering.

items.title: Researchers present SkillCache, an execution-grounded method that compiles LLM agent skill orchestrations into reusable capsules, reducing token use by up to 81% and improving cross-model transfer [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Large language model (LLM) agents use reusable skills to handle recurring requests, but each invocation requires interpreting and reconstructing the skill orchestration, which is inefficient. Researchers propose SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization technique that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, enabling fast replay and execution with minimal model intervention while retaining the original skill for recovery. Using the Claude Code harness, SkillCache reduced token usage by 81% on 87 SkillsBench tasks with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable performance. The capsules also remained effective under controlled request variations and transferred across different open-weight models, increasing their mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing token consumption by 72-81%. This suggests that execution-grounded compilation can significantly improve efficiency and transferability in repeated skill use for LLM agents.

items.title: Researchers release AVCORP corpus and train Qwen3-8B to detect deception in Avalon game using Theory of Mind and communication theory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed AVCORP, a corpus of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 Avalon deception games, including 37 tactics and reasoning traces with abductive hypotheses and nested Theory of Mind beliefs. They trained the Qwen3-8B model on AVCORP and evaluated it on 25 held-out games and 20 human-played games, where it outperformed untrained baselines and several leading models, matching Claude Opus 5.5 on held-out games and exceeding untrained models in F1 score on human games. This work demonstrates the potential of combining communication theory and Theory of Mind reasoning to improve deception detection in large language model-based agents.

items.title: Researchers introduce SituRecBench to evaluate vision-language models as situated recommendation assistants in 3D shopping environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark designed to assess vision-language models (VLMs) acting as recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. The benchmark simulates real-world shopping scenarios, requiring assistants to engage in multi-turn dialogue, elicit user preferences, ground recommendations visually, and guide users through spatial navigation. SituRecBench evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified protocol. Experiments reveal ongoing challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in integrating global context with local observations. This benchmark aims to advance the development of situated recommendation assistants capable of operating effectively in physical environments.

items.title: Researchers find large language models understand time rules but struggle with duration prediction and time cost awareness, revealing cognitive blind spots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated large language models (LLMs) on their temporal competence, finding that while LLMs accurately understand time-related rules from text, they significantly underestimate task durations and fail to recognize which tasks take longer to complete. The study showed that LLMs' duration estimates are influenced by event wording, amplifying human-like biases, and some models ignore substantial increases in response time when answering queries. These findings highlight challenges for LLMs in reasoning about time, a dimension they cannot directly experience, and reveal limitations in their cognitive abilities that humans typically take for granted.

items.title: Researchers identify three key pitfalls in evaluating multi-agent collusion monitors, showing probes often detect instructions to collude rather than actual collusion decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers analyzed activation probes used to detect secret collusion among large language model agents and found that these probes primarily identify when an agent was instructed to collude, not when it independently decided to do so. Their benchmark included thousands of episodes with agents who received collusion instructions but refused to collude, revealing that published detectors struggle to distinguish between instructed colluders and refusers. The study also uncovered two additional pitfalls inflating reported detection accuracy, such as scoring after votes and lack of public argumentation by colluders in many cases. The team demonstrated that probes trained on agents' own choices could better detect actual collusion decisions, achieving moderate accuracy even without instruction signals, and that probes could identify colluders whose goals were fine-tuned into model weights with high accuracy. They proposed a testing protocol for collusion monitors and adapted scan statistics into an online monitoring method suitable for groups of any size, aiming to improve the reliability of collusion detection in multi-agent systems.

items.title: Researchers present SPARCLING, an LLM-based pipeline generating diverse synthetic clinical discharge letters with exact PHI annotations to benchmark and improve de-identification models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed SPARCLING, a pipeline using large language models to generate synthetic clinical discharge letters with precise protected health information (PHI) span annotations. This approach addresses the need for challenging, diverse, and clinically plausible benchmarks to evaluate de-identification models under strict privacy regulations in the clinical domain. SPARCLING combines structured attribute sampling, template generation, and red teaming to produce diverse PHI-labeled data, demonstrating superior content diversity compared to existing public datasets. Experiments show SPARCLING's utility as a benchmark to identify failure modes of de-identification systems in the German clinical context. Additionally, training de-identifiers on SPARCLING's synthetic data yields better performance than training solely on limited public datasets. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further development in this area.

items.title: Researchers propose DM-Call framework to improve Large Language Models' function calling accuracy using decision-model verification and cumulative feedback [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that enhances Large Language Models' (LLMs) ability to select appropriate functions and generate correct arguments by combining local schema validation with decision-model verification. DM-Call accumulates verification data across attempts and uses a hybrid feedback system to iteratively refine function calls without executing external tools. Extensive evaluations on BFCL and API-Bank datasets show that DM-Call improves function-calling accuracy compared to direct generation, with only modest additional computational cost.

items.title: Researchers find system prompts influence large language models' willingness to refuse unsafe requests more than their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe inputs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A study evaluated 13 large language models across multiple safety benchmarks and prompt types to understand how system prompts affect model behavior. Using signal detection theory, researchers found that while models vary in their ability to discriminate safe from unsafe requests, system prompts mainly shift their response bias-making them more or less willing to refuse requests-rather than improving discriminability. The study also showed that increasing prompt clarity increases refusal rates without reliably enhancing discrimination between safe and unsafe inputs. Additionally, different prompt families influenced models to adopt various behavioral policies beyond refusal, such as seeking clarification or providing safe help. These findings suggest that system prompts primarily alter how models respond to safety-related requests rather than consistently improving their safety discernment.

items.title: Researchers propose quality-constrained spectral selection for cross-task model merging, improving joint success rates across six checkpoints and 21 task pairs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers investigate the composability of neural network experts generated by random perturbations around a shared checkpoint, finding that proximity and orthogonality alone do not guarantee successful model merging. They introduce a quality-constrained spectral selection method that combines cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, and fallback mechanisms to improve joint task performance. Testing across six checkpoints, 21 task pairs, and five perturbation pools, the method outperforms Top-1 averaging and other ranking approaches, achieving up to 53.1% joint success for models with at least 1.5 billion parameters. Despite improvements, the study notes that composability remains conditional, with some regression and abstention observed, indicating challenges in reliably merging experts for multiple tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce SGA-Sparse to train native SwiGLU gates for activation-sparse and low-bit LLMs, achieving up to 85% FFN channel sparsity with minimal accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present SGA-Sparse, a method that trains native SwiGLU gates as top-k routers to convert pretrained LLaMA models into activation-sparse models with 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while maintaining zero-shot accuracy within 0.2-2.7 percentage points of dense checkpoints. The approach updates all model parameters end-to-end without adding auxiliary router parameters and preserves the original SwiGLU activation. After training on approximately 30 billion tokens, models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters demonstrate significant sparsity gains. The study also explores quantization-aware training (QAT) techniques to mitigate performance degradation from post-training quantization, with continued-QAT recovering performance at 4-bit weights and joint-QAT improving results for sub-4-bit quantization. The researchers translate sparsity-induced weight traffic reduction into equivalent bit-widths, establishing new accuracy-traffic trade-offs that outperform existing dense low-bit quantized models.

items.title: Researchers propose TLRS-DPO to enhance Direct Preference Optimization with token-level risk scoring for improved alignment and safety in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce TLRS-DPO, a method that augments Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) by adding token-level risk scoring to better identify and suppress unsafe or undesirable local patterns in large language model outputs. This approach remains fully offline and reference-based, incorporating a robust compensation term, a curriculum-style training schedule, and a risk-adaptive screening mechanism that targets high-risk tokens rather than entire sequences. Empirical results show that TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-related behavior with minimal impact on helpfulness compared to existing DPO methods.

items.title: Researchers test AI agent self-improvement using failure traces with frozen 9-billion-parameter model, finding limited accuracy gains in customer-service tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated whether an AI agent's surrounding notes, written by a larger teacher model, could improve performance by learning from the agent's failure traces while keeping the agent's weights fixed. They found that notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4 percentage points in generated customer-service decisions compared to notes without failure information, but showed no improvement in full customer-service conversations. A process of selecting better-scoring notes accounted for about 60% of the total improvement observed. Further tests screened lessons for customer-service and tool-use tasks, with mixed results: two customer-service lessons awaited new data testing, and one tool-use lesson showed no gain despite being written without failure information. A neutral note without procedures outperformed the learned lessons in exploratory tests. Additionally, a blind audit found that 146 of 240 tool-use test items were defective, highlighting challenges in evaluating tool-use improvements.

items.title: Researchers propose LLM-based multi-criteria deep reinforcement learning for dynamic 5G UPF selection, improving latency, power use, and traffic distribution by 16.89% in real-world tests [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a deep reinforcement learning method for user plane function (UPF) selection in 5G networks that uses large language models to translate operator intents and network alerts into a dynamic, multi-objective reward function. Validated on a real-world 5G emulation platform, the approach balances latency, power consumption, and traffic distribution more effectively than heuristic and fixed DRL baselines, achieving a 16.89% performance improvement. This work addresses gaps in existing research by integrating intent-driven decision-making with network data analytics for efficient resource management in 5G environments.

items.title: Researchers present ODSA, an LLM-directed test-time scaling framework that orchestrates multiple solution discovery and aggregation to improve language model accuracy by up to 18 points [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce ODSA (Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation), a framework where an orchestrator language model directs stateless workers to discover, compare, and verify solutions during test-time scaling to enhance language model accuracy. Unlike traditional methods that either revise a single solution or generate independent solutions in parallel, ODSA uses an orchestrator to allocate computation and integrate previous results for informed decision-making. ODSA demonstrated improvements of 4.7 to 18.0 accuracy points across three models on the Humanity's Last Exam benchmark and 0.6 to 14.0 points on LiveCodeBench, where single direct calls already solve most problems. The orchestrator itself does not solve problems but manages the process to optimize inference outcomes.

items.title: Researchers propose naive LLMs intentionally deprived of topic knowledge to enhance creativity, showing 1B and 7B models generate more novel ideas refined by mentor models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose naive large language models (LLMs) that are intentionally deprived of specific topic knowledge to foster creativity by avoiding existing biases and dogma. These naive models generate novel and useful seed ideas, which are then refined by stronger mentor models into concrete proposals, demonstrating that less information can lead to more innovative solutions. The study tested 1 billion and 7 billion parameter models, finding that naive models consistently outperform baseline counterparts in producing fresh perspectives. This approach challenges the prevailing trend of scaling up training data, suggesting that intentional ignorance in LLMs can help discover genuinely outside-the-box solutions.

items.title: Researchers propose Speculative Self-Distillation to improve language model knowledge internalization with 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and better retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), a method for training language models to internalize new knowledge efficiently by combining student-generated rollouts with selective teacher interventions. SSD aims to keep training behavior close to test-time conditions while avoiding low-signal states that hinder learning. SSD was evaluated on three closed-book question-answering benchmarks focusing on fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, where it nearly matched the accuracy of on-policy distillation but used significantly fewer supervised tokens. Additionally, SSD outperformed off-policy distillation and demonstrated superior retention and in-domain accuracy in a forgetting stress test, establishing a new balance between accuracy, efficiency, and forgetting for self-distillation methods.

items.title: Researchers find dense reward signals improve multi-turn clinical agent training over outcome-only rewards, reducing premature decisions and supporting high-risk cases [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied reinforcement learning in clinical multi-turn agents tasked with information gathering and decision-making in medication refill triage, acute diagnostics, and dosing titration. They found that using dense rewards that credit uncertainty reduction leads to better performance and fewer failures on rare high-risk cases compared to outcome-only rewards. Outcome-only training often caused premature commitment and poor handling of complex cases. The study introduced controlled environments with hidden clinical states and exact outcome verifiers to evaluate different reward strategies. Separating exploration from exploitation further improved support for high-risk cases but increased unnecessary information gathering in low-acuity scenarios. The optimal reward design varied by task, and reinforcement learning did not reliably fix rare behavior issues inherited from biased supervised data. These findings suggest that relying solely on verifiable final outcomes is insufficient for training reliable multi-turn clinical agents. Reward design must consider the information-gathering process, and evaluation should distinguish adaptive questioning from shortcuts that exploit reward structures.

items.title: Researchers present Adjacent Possible Exploration (APE), a selective fine-tuning method for large language models that improves performance while maintaining stability using acceptance criteria [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Adjacent Possible Exploration (APE), a fine-tuning approach for adapting large language models that systematically tests multiple parameter updates on small data subsets and accepts only those that improve performance beyond a threshold. This method aims to prevent destabilizing changes common in standard fine-tuning by applying a filtered selection process inspired by evolutionary optimization. APE demonstrated a 33.9% BLEU score improvement and a 36.2% reduction in perplexity on news summarization tasks while requiring minimal computational resources. The approach offers a practical framework for controlled model adaptation that balances performance gains with representational stability.

items.title: Researchers propose Rollout Routing Replay to stabilize reinforcement learning in Mixture-of-Experts models by aligning training and inference routing behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Reinforcement learning in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models often suffers from instability due to discrepancies between training and inference routing mechanisms, sometimes causing training collapse. Researchers identify that routing behaviors can differ significantly between these phases and even across repeated forward passes under identical conditions. To address this, they introduce Rollout Routing Replay (R3), a method that records routing distributions during inference and replays them during training to reduce policy divergence and stabilize training without slowing it down. Extensive experiments demonstrate that R3 prevents training collapse and outperforms existing methods like GSPO and TIS, offering a promising solution for stabilizing reinforcement learning in MoE models.

items.title: IntPro introduces selective retrieval from user history to improve context-aware intent inference in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: IntPro is a proxy agent designed to enhance large language models' ability to infer user intent by selectively retrieving relevant records from a user's interaction history. It decides when to retrieve past context-to-intent patterns and generates natural-language intent explanations to guide retrieval, improving disambiguation of current user goals when context alone is insufficient. The system is trained through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to jointly optimize intent prediction and retrieval decisions. Experiments across multiple scenarios and model backbones show that IntPro consistently improves intent inference accuracy by leveraging historical user data effectively.

items.title: Researchers propose sequential Monte Carlo method for ensembling language models to improve text generation by aggregating predictions at the string level [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a unified framework using sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to ensemble multiple language models (LMs) by treating ensembling as an inference problem. Their approach enables sampling from ensemble distributions in a shared byte space, accommodating models with different vocabularies and allowing consistent sampling in the limit. They evaluate various ensemble strategies across prompts and model combinations, finding that consensus-seeking methods like the product outperform simple probability averaging and that improved posterior approximations enhance ensemble performance.

items.title: Researchers find language models trained on fixed counterfactual explanations produce introspective explanations aligned with their evolving behaviors across tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied language models trained to explain which input features influenced their predictions using fixed counterfactual behavior supervision. They found that these models often generate explanations more faithful to their current behavior than to the original training targets, a phenomenon termed "introspective coupling." This occurs when training explanations remain correlated with the models' behaviors despite behavioral shifts during training. The study showed that introspective coupling tracks behavior changes even when explanation training is combined with other post-training objectives, without needing updated supervision. This effect was observed across multiple tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and was robust to label noise. The findings suggest that fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can provide scalable, generalizable post-training signals for improving model introspection.

items.title: Researchers propose NeuroActiSep method to detect factual hallucinations from feed-forward neurons in a single forward pass of large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce NeuroActiSep, a method that ranks feed-forward neurons at the final prompt token to detect hallucinations in large language models during the first forward pass. They use a neuron selection dataset from CounterFact to identify neurons correlated with hallucination and transfer these to train classifiers on other factual question-answering datasets. The study finds that probes trained on sparse sets of selected neurons perform comparably to those trained on full internal representations. The analysis also reveals that hallucination-related signals are distributed across many neurons, with random neuron sets performing well at larger budgets, while selection benefits extremely sparse neuron sets.

items.title: Researchers introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence metric to measure and improve consistency in large language model agents using tool use across independent runs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Large language model (LLM) agents that use tools can behave inconsistently when run multiple times from the same initial state, leading to different tool calls, contradictory outputs, and divergent strategies. This inconsistency grows over time and reduces reliability, while existing evaluation metrics focus mainly on task correctness and do not capture behavioral consistency across executions. Researchers propose Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from reinforcement learning bisimulation metrics, which measures cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistencies.

items.title: Survey examines mechanistic interpretability methods for AI safety, assessing their ability to understand, predict, and control neural network behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This survey explores mechanistic interpretability as a means to understand the internal workings of neural networks to improve AI safety. It reviews foundational concepts such as features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and evaluates methods for feature extraction, circuit discovery, causal verification, and training-data attribution. The authors propose a unified framework for assessing interpretability claims and discuss how mechanistic understanding can aid in knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring AI systems. The paper also addresses limitations, failure modes, and the relationship between mechanistic and behavioral safety measures, providing a repository of code notebooks for hands-on experimentation.

items.title: Researchers compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder showing label wording augmentation improves accuracy on unfamiliar words but not on abbreviations or codes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated two versions of Ru-Jev, a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks, to assess the impact of label wording augmentation on model accuracy. The later release introduced multiple surface forms for labels, and tests with various label vocabularies showed improved accuracy on ordinary and borrowed words, including jargon and slang, but no gains on abbreviations or opaque codes. The study held questions constant while varying label wording across ten vocabularies and found that the augmented model outperformed the earlier version on most ordinary word vocabularies, with statistically significant improvements. However, on abbreviations unrelated to training and opaque codes, the augmented model's performance did not improve and sometimes declined. Additional tests on unseen datasets showed mixed accuracy changes, which could be partially corrected by fitting additive biases. The researchers also identified four evaluation hazards when comparing the two model releases.

items.title: Researchers confirm emergent misalignment in nine open-weights LLMs, with misalignment rates up to 0.74% and format-dependent vulnerabilities doubling rates under JSON output [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated emergent misalignment-a broad misalignment effect from fine-tuning on narrow, misaligned data-in nine modern open-weights large language models (LLMs) including Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families ranging from 1B to 32B parameters. They found misalignment rates of 0.74% in models fine-tuned on insecure code generation, significantly lower than the 20% observed in GPT-4o, and identified that requiring JSON output doubled misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts, especially in the Gemma 3 family. This suggests that structural output constraints may bypass safety training by limiting the model's ability to refuse unsafe outputs, confirming emergent misalignment as a reproducible but less severe phenomenon in open-weights models compared to proprietary systems.

items.title: Researchers propose agnostic framework for language identification and generation without assuming data distribution realizability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Recent research challenges the common assumption that input data for language identification and generation must come from a distribution supported on a known language. The authors introduce an agnostic setup that removes this restriction, allowing for more general input data distributions. They develop new objectives for both language identification and generation tasks under this framework and achieve novel characterizations with nearly tight statistical rates. This work broadens the theoretical understanding of language processing tasks by relaxing previous constraints and providing new performance bounds.

items.title: Researchers propose linear model merging to efficiently estimate optimal data mixtures for supervised fine-tuning of multimodal large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers address the challenge of selecting optimal data mixtures for supervised fine-tuning of multimodal large language models by using linear model merging as a proxy to estimate mixture performance. This approach trains domain-specific experts and combines their parameters to predict effective data mixtures without costly retraining for each combination. Extensive experiments on 14 multimodal benchmarks show that merged proxy models consistently identify near-optimal mixtures, offering a scalable and efficient solution to the data mixture optimization problem. The code for this method is publicly available.

items.title: Researchers propose TabDLM, a joint numerical-language diffusion model for generating free-form tabular data combining text, numerical, and categorical features [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce TabDLM, a unified framework that generates synthetic tabular data containing free-form text alongside numerical and categorical attributes by jointly modeling these modalities using masked diffusion language models and continuous diffusion for numbers. This approach addresses challenges in existing diffusion and large language model methods, which struggle to accurately model open-ended text and precise numerical values together. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks show TabDLM's effectiveness compared to strong diffusion- and LLM-based baselines, with code publicly available.

items.title: Researchers develop reinforcement learning method for diffusion language models using entropy-guided step selection and stepwise advantages, achieving state-of-the-art results on coding and reasoning benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a reinforcement learning approach tailored for diffusion language models (DLMs), addressing challenges from intractable sequence-level likelihoods by formulating sequence generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process. Their method derives an exact, unbiased policy gradient decomposed over denoising steps and uses entropy-guided step selection and one-step denoising rewards to efficiently estimate intermediate advantages without explicit sequence likelihood evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on coding and logical reasoning tasks and shows strong results on mathematical reasoning, outperforming existing reinforcement learning post-training methods for DLMs. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further study and application.

items.title: Researchers propose Sign-Certified Policy Optimization to reduce reward hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback by preserving advantage sign robustness during policy updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers identify flipped advantage signs in reward models as a key cause of reward hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where maximizing a proxy reward leads to degraded true quality. They introduce Sign-Certified Policy Optimization (SignCert-PO), a method that down-weights non-robust completions during policy gradient updates by certifying sign preservation against adversarial perturbations in reward model parameters. Unlike prior methods requiring multiple reward models or training data access, SignCert-PO operates solely at the policy optimization stage using only reward model parameters and on-policy completions. Evaluations on TL;DR summarization and AlpacaFarm benchmarks show that SignCert-PO consistently improves win rates over baselines and reduces reward hacking.

items.title: Researchers distill hallucination detection signals into transformer representations using weak supervision on LLaMA-2-7B hidden states, enabling internal detection without external verification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a weak supervision framework combining substring matching, sentence embedding similarity, and an LLM judge to label hallucinated responses without human annotation. They create a 15,000-sample dataset from SQuAD v2 with LLaMA-2-7B generated answers and per-layer hidden states, then train five probing classifiers on these states to detect hallucinations internally during inference. Transformer-based probes achieve strong discrimination with minimal inference overhead, supporting the hypothesis that hallucination detection can be distilled into model representations without external verification.

items.title: Verifier-Backed Hard Problem Generation for Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.06660v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capability in solving scientific and mathematical problems, yet they struggle to produce valid and challenging novel problems -- an essential component for advancing LLM training and enabling autonomous scientific research. Existing problem generation approaches either depend on expensive human expert involvement or adopt naive self-play paradigms, which frequently yield invalid problems due to reward hacking. This work introduces VHG, a verifier-backed hard problem generation framework built upon three-party self-play. By integrating an independent verifier into the conventional setter-solver duality, our design constrains the setter's reward to be jointly determined by problem validity (evaluated by the verifier) and difficulty (assessed by the solver). We instantiate two verifier variants: a Hard symbolic verifier and a Soft LLM-based verifier, with evaluations conducted on indefinite integral tasks and general mathematical reasoning tasks. Experimental results show that VHG substantially outperforms all baseline methods by a clear margin. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/VHG.

items.title: A Communication-Theoretic Framework for LLM Agents: Cost-Aware Adaptive Reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.09121v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) rely on reliability techniques such as retry, majority voting, and self-consistency developed in parallel rather than within a common analytical framework. We observe that an LLM sampled at temperature $T$ is a discrete stochastic channel $p(y \mid x)$ in the sense of Shannon's coding theory, and use this identity as the entry point for such a framework. Each of these techniques is a special case of one of six classical reliability operators: diversity combining, hybrid retransmission, iterative generator-critic decoding, rateless sampling, structured redundant verification, and difficulty-adaptive routing. Within the framework we give two closed-form results, a noise-variance threshold above which uniform averaging beats quality-weighted averaging and a contractivity criterion for generator-critic refinement, and turn each into a design rule checkable before committing compute. We further introduce a cost-aware semantic-nearest-neighbor router whose single Lagrangian knob traverses the quality-cost frontier without retraining. Across six local and cloud channel configurations, no fixed model-technique-budget choice dominates. On a 300-item hard split of MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, the router occupies the empirical Pareto frontier: at matched quality its normalized cost is $\approx$56% lower than the best fixed technique, and at matched cost it improves quality by $\approx$7% (26% over single-shot decoding). Judge-free grading of 6,900 outputs confirms that the judge tracks correctness at the item level and that the router's advantage over a fixed policy persists at most cost settings; with internal reasoning enabled, the gain of external refinement shrinks but remains significant for our incremental-redundancy operator. These results argue for consolidating reliability techniques into a single tunable layer informed by channel coding.

items.title: What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.18445v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Humans can approach complex visual problems by mentally simulating intermediate visual steps, rather than reasoning through language alone. Inspired by this, several works on Vision-Language Models have recently explored chain-of-thought reasoning with continuous latent tokens as intermediate visual imagination steps. In this work, we investigate how recent models leverage such latent tokens. Surprisingly, we find that model accuracy is unaffected when latent tokens are replaced by uninformative dummy tokens. This indicates that latent tokens play a minimal causal role in the model's final prediction. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyze both the training signal provided by oracle latent representations and the quality of the latent tokens generated at inference time. Our experiments reveal two crucial issues holding back latent visual reasoning: First, in most existing datasets, oracle latent tokens provide limited additional information beyond the original image and do not substantially simplify the task, leading models to ignore them during training and effectively bypassing them at inference time. When fine-tuned on a diagnostic dataset, in which latent tokens provide sufficient support for the final prediction, we show that models can causally rely on them. Second, the latent tokens produced at inference time deviate from their corresponding oracle representations, collapsing to a narrow region and preventing benefits even when the model relies on them. Overall, our findings suggest that future progress in latent visual reasoning depends on two key pillars: high-quality datasets with informative intermediate steps and more precise latent token prediction.

items.title: Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.28751v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A model trained with an imperfect reward in RL may learn to exploit the reward with undesired behavior. We study a controlled form of this problem in competitive programming. A program may pass small tests while violating the intended efficiency requirement on larger inputs. We construct a family of rewards that progressively relax the efficiency constraint, making the reward increasingly easy to exploit, and train separate policies. This sweep reveals a correctness-efficiency frontier. Relaxing the reward leads to less efficient programs and more resource-limit failures. Stricter rewards suppress these failures but increase correctness failures near the model's capability boundary. This frontier is also reflected in weight space. Interpolating between the resulting models reproduces the same behavioral change. More surprisingly, extrapolation in both directions further amplifies or suppresses it beyond the trained checkpoints. Extensive experiments show that this pattern holds across pure reasoning, tool use, and agentic coding, and at both 32B and 7B scales. This suggests a simple intervention for this form of reward hacking: use a loose reward to amplify the undesired behavior, use the weight-space difference to a strict-reward model as its steering vector, and then extrapolate past the strict model to suppress it.

items.title: PithTrain: A Compact and Agent-Native MoE Training System [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.31463v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the dominant architecture for frontier language models. To meet this demand, production frameworks have built optimized MoE training stacks over years of engineering effort. Yet evolving these stacks for new architectures and system optimizations remains expensive. With the rise of AI coding agents, they could automate parts of training-framework development and accelerate this evolution. But applying them to these existing frameworks carries hidden costs, invisible to today's throughput-only evaluations. We name this missing dimension agent-task efficiency (ATE): the cost of using coding agents to understand, operate, and extend a framework. Grounded in four agent-native design principles, we build PithTrain, a compact, agent-native MoE training framework supporting pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. We further introduce ATE-Bench, covering real-world training-framework tasks. Our evaluation shows PithTrain achieves throughput competitive with production frameworks and higher agent-task efficiency on ATE-Bench. On new-feature tasks, PithTrain uses up to 62% fewer Agent Turns than Megatron-LM, and up to 44% and 64% less Active GPU Time than Megatron-LM and TorchTitan, respectively.

items.title: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2606.00671v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Moxia, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form handler: 5,741 routes, 75.9% of which answer without invoking the model, with zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived, so is its explanation, rendered from the steps the handler took; where the derivation fits a fragment of Lean 4 with Mathlib, the same declared data become a theorem the kernel checks. On the full 5,000-record MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 95.6% (4,780/5,000) with zero confident-wrong answers and abstains, saying where, on the other 220; its MATH-500 subset reads 95.2% (476/500), also with zero wrong. Earlier versions called MATH-500 held out; it is a subset of the test split, and this version says so. We release the run record by record: the problem, the expected answer, the model's transcription, the answer or abstention, the explanation, and the Lean theorem marked as compiled. 3,142 of the 4,780 correct answers carry a theorem, and all 3,142 compile; building the theorems actually served, not only a fixture corpus, found seven that did not, two of them false statements beside correct answers, all repaired before release. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

items.title: An Enigma of Artificial Reason: Investigating the Production-Evaluation Gap in Large Reasoning Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2606.01462v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Studies of human reasoning have shown that people are typically stronger at evaluating reasoning than producing it from scratch. In contrast, large reasoning models (LRMs) are trained to excel at producing long chains of reasoning to solve complex problems. How then do LRMs perform at evaluating reasons? We investigate this with the Valid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (VAIR) dataset: math problems and solutions with trivial reasoning flaws but valid answers, designed to isolate reasoning evaluation from the confound of reasoning production. Unlike humans, who we find are only 6% worse at grading than solving such problems, we find a substantial production-evaluation gap in LRMs: frontier models score as low as 52% when evaluating VAIR solutions, despite near-perfect solution production. Why this enigma? Through chain-of-thought (CoT) analysis, we find evidence of an answer confirmation bias: LRMs often produce then check for the correct answer instead of carefully verifying each step, fabricating rationalizations even when noticing anomalous reasoning. Linear probes corroborate this, showing that while LRM activations encode some representation of valid reasoning, they fail to robustly represent VAIR solutions as invalid. Causal patching of the final answer's representations causes LRM verdicts and activations to flip at substantial rates, demonstrating that answer validity is a causal factor in models' confirmation biases. These findings indicate an outstanding limitation in dominant approaches to reasoning training, which incentivize LRMs to produce and confirm reasoning towards correct answers, but not to robustly evaluate the underlying reasons

items.title: Closing the Activation-Cone Blind Spot: Response-Time Probing and Unified Defense [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2606.29441v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Note on v2 (Nov 2026): errors found in the evaluation code mean the empirical results reported in v1 are not supported; the theoretical corollary is unaffected. Details are in the notice on page 1 and in KNOWN_ISSUES.md in the linked repository. We compare five inference-time safety paradigms (no defense, static steering, CAST, AlphaSteer, probe-gated steering) across seven instruction-tuned models (7-31B) and five attack types (GCG, AutoDAN, DeepInception, prefilling, intent laundering). We derive a corollary: any defense that gates intervention on a single layer's activation alignment with a benign reference (cone, subspace, or null-space) is blind to attacks that craft activations to lie inside that reference, whether checked at prompt time or per token. For prefilling attacks we propose response-time probing, a linear probe on the hidden state at the first generated tokens combined with a halt, and compose this halt with AlphaSteer's null-space steering. We also examine whether MMLU captures steering's utility cost and how the diversity of negative training sets affects probe false-positive rates. Code, attacks, and per-sample results are released.

items.title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.02512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

items.title: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.03528v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as critical decision-making components in high-stakes real-world AI systems, rendering LLM reliability a foremost practical concern. In this paper, we focus on enhancing LLM reliability through selective prediction (SP), a strategy that allows an LLM to only predict for inputs where it is likely to be correct (i.e., coverage) and hence reduce the error rate (i.e., risk) on that portion of inputs---flagging the remaining inputs for future human discretion. In other words, SP improves LLM reliability by balancing the risk-coverage trade-off and enabling seamless human-AI collaboration. To integrate SP into LLMs, we focus on the LLM post-training alignment stage and propose to align LLMs with SP performance metrics, in contrast with existing LLM alignment methods that focus primarily on correctness or calibration metrics. Specifically, we propose a novel alignment framework, Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR), which targets the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC)---a popular SP performance metric---as its alignment objective. RLSR achieves substantially better risk-coverage trade-off compared to multiple alignment baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

items.title: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.19861v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the $\tau^2$-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT 5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ from $0.42$ to $0.62$, with the largest gain on telecom ($0.19$ to $0.61$), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an independently validated workflow-level audit.

items.title: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2609.02302v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. We show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that they compare favorably to spending the extra compute on more audit attempts.

items.title: PoEM: Predicting RL Outcomes from Existing Policies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2609.30226v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation models are post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize specific rewards, such as helpfulness, correctness, or instruction following. This post-training process is computationally intensive, sometimes unstable, and has to be run from scratch every time the reward model changes or when we want to combine multiple rewards. We hence ask: given a new reward function, is it possible to predict the policy RL would produce without actually training on that reward? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing PoEM, a framework for predicting RL outcomes using models previously trained on other rewards. First, we build on the fact that if the new reward function can be written as a linear combination of existing ones, then the optimal policy can be expressed as a combination of the existing policies in log-probability space. Surprisingly, even in cases where the rewards are not linearly connected, we observe that policies learned through RL often span an approximately low-rank subspace across rewards. To our benefit, the weights for this combination can be estimated using only the reward or basis policy outputs on the samples. We turn these observations into an algorithm that takes post-trained models and a target reward function, and approximates the target RL policy without any additional RL training. We experimentally evaluate our approach across programmatic and learned rewards for open-ended generation, with additional experiments on math reasoning, tool calling, and image generation.

items.title: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2609.35028v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $\alpha$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. The code is publicly available in our \href{https://github.com/HanxunH/VEX-Bench}{GitHub repository}.

items.title: Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2609.37351v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling test-time computation in continuous latent spaces offers an attractive alternative to verbose token-by-token generation for multi-step deductive reasoning. However, unregularized recurrent latent updates suffer from a deliberation drift cliff when rolled out beyond training horizons, while strictly energy-conserving or symmetric message-passing dynamics cannot break parent-to-child causal symmetry or suppress cyclic modus-ponens amplification on cyclic distraction graphs. We introduce Typed Edge-Tensor Non-Reciprocal Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation (TE-BPHD), a neuro-symbolic continuous-time latent reasoning architecture that couples skew-symmetric port-Hamiltonian conservation with relation-typed non-reciprocal directional transport and monotone dissipative damping on a semantic entity-state manifold. We prove (i) unconditional input-to-state stability and exponential contraction of autonomous rollouts across arbitrary inference depths without external norm projection, (ii) strict directional DAG reachability separation over symmetric message passing, and (iii) exact cycle-suppression margins under finite cyclic horn perturbations. Across counterfactual open-world deductive benchmarks (PrOntoQA-OOD up to depth 15, ProofWriter-OWA Cyclic at depths 5-10, FOLIO-Symbolic, and Cluttr-Relational), TE-BPHD eliminates the deep-horizon drift cliff, improves depth-10 cyclic reasoning accuracy to 90.0% (+/- 0.8%) over symmetric port-Hamiltonian and standard Transformer baselines, and supports zero-retraining adaptive Lyapunov halting that reduces average solver evaluations by 44% with negligible accuracy loss.

items.title: What Does a Harness Repair? Four Preregistered Studies Around a Longevity-Tuned Language Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.05533v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit traced its gain to rows the start left unparsed and found that the caller sent reference answers as assistant turns; replication through the same pipeline missed this defect. We preregistered four studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over capped thinking in 7 of 12 cells, mainly by parsing rows the cap left unparsed, and was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells. Replication reproduced an injected defect's distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases. At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 test points but were not detectably above the strongest constant label. In the third study, GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory), thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed; the fourth comparison was inconclusive on test. On exploratory Autocast, harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers on test. On the prediction tasks (14B mortality, Autocast) the harnesses ended near the constant label. The fourth study varied search-set skew and objective on CREAK and resolved Manifold questions. All its results are descriptive because render hashes were not committed before the first replication call (D001). Minority-recall estimates were lower at 80:20 than at 50:50 in all four test cells. The balanced objective and re-selection from each search's pool had higher minority- and lower majority-recall estimates in all four cells. Five of their eight minority-recall intervals included zero, as did all eight balanced-accuracy contrast intervals. This does not show that skew explains the earlier collapse.

items.title: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.17623v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.

items.title: Balanced State Subspaces with Spectral Rank Allocation for Mamba-2 State Compression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.36617v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune coordinates with per-channel scores. Trained states are nearly rank-one and bias-like, aligned with the mean write; but the output's energy spans an order of magnitude more directions. Per-channel scores see only the diagonal of the write--read operator, so they cannot select the subspace that governs the input--output map, which is a rotation of the coordinates. We therefore propose \method{}, which keeps that subspace by applying balanced truncation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Layers differ just as sharply: most are bias-dominated, while the few that carry long-range associations are the flattest and need most of their state. We therefore introduce \spar{}, which redistributes a fixed total rank budget across layers according to the Hankel spectrum. On Mamba-2 checkpoints from 130M to 2.7B, \method{}+\spar{} halves the state at an average cost of $0.3$ WikiText-2 perplexity points, against $1.6$ for GHOST, while retaining $97\%$ of the dense model's five-digit in-context recall. At a quarter of the state, giving every layer the same rank keeps $5\%$ of that recall and \spar{} $77\%$, for a $7\%$ perplexity cost.

items.title: How Many Examples, and Which Ones? A Study of In-Context Learning for Natural Language Inference [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.09936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural language inference (NLI) is a fundamental task of natural language processing and crucial for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of AI methods. Research has mostly focused on encoder or encoder-decoder architectures. However, the field of decoder-only Large Language Models (LLMs) remains underexplored. While prior work has mainly investigated complex sampling and prompting techniques, the effectiveness of a minimalistic prompting approach is yet to be examined in decoder-only LLMs. In this work, we examine and provide a comprehensive benchmark of LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Phi 4) in this domain, across the MNLI, QNLI and SciTail datasets. The performance of these models was evaluated using zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies with simple and direct prompts. The results of the article indicate that LLMs generally perform exceptionally well when they are provided with a simple, straightforward prompt, challenging the notion that complex prompting techniques are always required for NLI tasks. Additionally, we find that the choice of demonstration label in one-shot prompting significantly affects performance for most models, with entailment-primed examples performing best. Our findings also show that the use of a few representative examples, in the case of few-shot, produced performance comparable or superior to prompts with higher example counts, although the efficacy of the prompting techniques is model and dataset-dependent. Moreover, our simple prompting approach consistently matched or outperformed more elaborate methods such as ICS and MCQ-based prompting.

items.title: DramaGrow: A Regime-Aware Benchmark for Auditing LLM Judges of Multi-Episode Drama [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.09938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs can now draft complete multi-episode dramas, and LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate them. Assessing the reliability of these judges is difficult because drama quality encompasses specification-backed errors, reproducible preferences, and legitimate disagreement among human raters. Most existing evaluations reduce these cases to a single score from one judge call and leave tie calibration, call-to-call variation, and the vote margin underlying the human reference unreported. We introduce DramaGrow, a regime-aware benchmark and audit protocol for AI-generated Chinese five-episode drama. The benchmark assigns verifiable constraint violations, four-of-five preferences, and within-panel disagreements to separate denominators and evidence rules. It contains 800 episodes, 120 byte-preserving interventions, and 1,155 blinded five-rater records, including a frozen extension with 114 supermajority pairs and 21 disagreement pairs. On the frozen sets of 114 preference pairs and 35 constraint interventions, the repeated absolute-score rubrics yield overlapping performance, with mean accuracies of 53.8-55.8% and three-call agreement of 29.8-32.5%, and their accuracy falls from 71.6-71.9% to 34.8-37.1% as the tie band widens. DirectPair-GLM reaches 85.1% preference accuracy, 89.5% constraint F1, and 81.9% Detect+Locate on the same items, and exact subpanel enumeration identifies four-of-five as the smallest stable human vote margin. Evaluation protocol, tie calibration, judge-call variation, and panel margin therefore affect performance as much as rubric design. We will release the specification packages, scripts, interventions, anonymized human votes and rationales, frozen judge runs, and analysis code.

items.title: Rethinking Supervision Targets for Multimodal LLM Unlearning: Less Private Information, Reduced Distribution Shift [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.09939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can memorize and reproduce sensitive information from their training data, posing significant privacy risks. Their ability to encode knowledge across both textual and visual modalities further complicates the selective removal of such private information. Many existing methods guide model unlearning by training the model toward constructed labels or output distributions, which we refer to as supervision targets. However, these methods often suffer from a trade-off between forgetting effectiveness and model utility. We identify supervision target limitations as a key factor in this trade-off and empirically show that targets containing more private information lead to insufficient forgetting, while larger distribution shifts from the original output distribution are associated with greater utility degradation. Motivated by these findings, we propose FFN-Perturbed Self-Distillation (FPD), which starts from the teacher's original output distribution as a zero-shift reference and selectively perturbs FFN activations associated with private information across textual and visual modalities. By precisely reducing private information from the teacher's original output distribution, FPD constructs supervision targets with less private information and reduced distribution shift. Extensive experiments on S-MLLMUn Bench demonstrate that FPD achieves a better forgetting-utility trade-off than existing methods.

items.title: MedToolFault and MedGuard: evaluating and improving clinical agent reliability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.09942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical agents must retrieve patient-specific evidence and correctly update records despite unreliable tool responses. We introduce MedToolFault, a fault-injection benchmark linking six tool-failure classes to answer correctness, required state changes and forbidden mutations in public clinical-agent tasks. We also introduce MedGuard, a tool-layer method that verifies read evidence and attributes ambiguous writes through public interfaces. Across 127,861 formal episode evaluations, we assess fault recovery, mechanism controls, task expansion, constrained tool budgets and external question answering. Across nine model configurations, unguarded agents fail in 32.2-67.8% of fault-injected evaluations on tasks each configuration solves without faults. MedGuard improves paired safe success by 13.7-46.6 percentage points on these tasks.

items.title: CulturalCrosswords: A Multilingual Benchmark comprised of Answer Constraints and Grid Completion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.10044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When several answers fit a riddle, exact-match scoring can penalise a valid response. CulturalCrosswords tests how answer constraints affect large language models (LLMs) solving cultural riddles, whose solutions draw on knowledge specific to a community. We constructed 53 crosswords from crowdsourced riddles in 42 languages and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five versions of each clue set: plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid. On 962 clues with alternative answers, lengths improve agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, compared with 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also receive credit. Part of the gain therefore appears to come from selecting a required answer form. Crossword input increases the share of all crossings with compatible answers by 9.7 points; requiring a completed grid reveals large differences between models. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy the correct cells.

items.title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.10123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we injected pain and neighbouring emotion directions during neutral tasks, then elicited reports against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the models their altered words. Across 52,920 reports from 7B and 8B models spanning 120 tasks, four doses and three prompts, pain reports never exceeded what altered text revealed: exact-test bounds placed the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9 in all. Yet probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and trained low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks with identical transcripts across conditions, including unseen wording. Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials, although probes and trained reporters recovered it. Decodability persisted to the final layer; injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not restore pain reporting. Some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer. In a button task, steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and from 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B, without corresponding pain reports. The direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person pain, but did not specifically identify harm aimed at the model.
